Imputation
im-pyoo-TAY-shun
noun (Reformed soteriology)
From Latin imputare (to reckon, charge to one's account); Greek logizomai (to reckon, count, impute). The Reformed-confessional doctrine that God credits or reckons something to a person's account that is not inherently theirs: Adam's sin imputed to his posterity, the believer's sin imputed to Christ, and Christ's righteousness imputed to the believer. The threefold imputation that structures Reformed soteriology.

See also: Imputation

📖 Biblical Definition

From Latin imputare (to reckon, charge to one's account); the Reformed-confessional doctrine that God credits or reckons something to a person's account that is not inherently their own. The Greek logizomai (to reckon, count, impute) is the key NT term, used eleven times in Romans 4 alone. The doctrine involves a threefold imputation that structures the whole of Reformed soteriology. (1) The imputation of Adam's sin to his posterity: Adam's first sin is reckoned to the account of all his natural descendants, so that all are born guilty and corrupt in him (Romans 5:12-19; the doctrine of original sin). (2) The imputation of the believer's sin to Christ: the sins of God's people are reckoned to Christ's account, so that He bore their guilt and its penalty on the cross (Isaiah 53:6, the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all; 2 Corinthians 5:21, he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; 1 Peter 2:24, who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree). (3) The imputation of Christ's righteousness to the believer: the perfect righteousness of Christ (His active obedience to the law and His passive obedience in bearing its penalty) is reckoned to the account of the believing sinner, so that he is justified — declared righteous — not on the basis of his own righteousness but on the basis of Christ's righteousness imputed to him (Romans 4:3-8, Abraham's faith counted for righteousness; 2 Corinthians 5:21, that we might be made the righteousness of God in him; Philippians 3:9, the righteousness which is of God by faith). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive threefold imputation as the structural backbone of Reformed soteriology: condemned through Adam's imputed sin; redeemed through our sin imputed to Christ; justified through Christ's righteousness imputed to us. The doctrine of imputation (especially the imputation of Christ's righteousness) is the heart of the Reformation doctrine of justification, denied by Rome (which holds justification to be by infused, not imputed, righteousness) and by the New Perspective on Paul (which reframes justification as covenant-membership status).

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Reformed-confessional doctrine that God reckons to a person's account something not inherently theirs; threefold: Adam's sin imputed to his posterity (Romans 5:12-19), the believer's sin imputed to Christ (2 Corinthians 5:21; Isaiah 53:6), Christ's righteousness imputed to the believer (Romans 4:3-8; Philippians 3:9); the structural backbone of Reformed soteriology.

IMPUTATION, n. (Reformed soteriology; Latin imputare, to reckon; Greek logizomai) God reckons to a person's account something not inherently their own. Threefold: (1) Adam's sin imputed to his posterity (Romans 5:12-19; original sin). (2) The believer's sin imputed to Christ (Isaiah 53:6; 2 Corinthians 5:21, he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; 1 Peter 2:24). (3) Christ's righteousness imputed to the believer (Romans 4:3-8; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Philippians 3:9, the righteousness which is of God by faith). The structural backbone of Reformed soteriology: condemned through Adam's imputed sin; redeemed through our sin imputed to Christ; justified through Christ's righteousness imputed to us. Denied by Rome (infused, not imputed, righteousness) and the New Perspective.

📖 Key Scripture

Romans 4:5-6 — "But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness. Even as David also describeth the blessedness of the man, unto whom God imputeth righteousness without works."

2 Corinthians 5:21 — "For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him."

Isaiah 53:6 — "All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way; and the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all."

Philippians 3:9 — "And be found in him, not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, the righteousness which is of God by faith."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Imputation (especially of Christ's righteousness) is the heart of the Reformation doctrine of justification; denied by Rome (justification by infused righteousness) and by the New Perspective on Paul (justification as covenant-membership status).

expand to see more

The doctrine of imputation, especially the imputation of Christ's righteousness, is the heart of the Reformation doctrine of justification, and it is denied by two principal positions. The Roman Catholic position holds that justification is by infused righteousness, not imputed righteousness: God does not merely reckon Christ's righteousness to the believer's account (declaring him righteous) but infuses righteousness into the believer (making him actually righteous), so that justification is a process of becoming righteous rather than a declaration of righteous standing; this confuses justification with sanctification and grounds the believer's standing partly in his own infused-and-cooperated-with righteousness. The New Perspective on Paul reframes justification as covenant-membership status (the declaration that one is a member of the covenant people) rather than the imputation of Christ's righteousness, denying or marginalizing the imputation of Christ's active obedience. The Reformed-confessional tradition holds the substantive imputation doctrine: justification is the forensic declaration that the believing sinner is righteous, on the basis of Christ's righteousness imputed (reckoned) to his account through faith; the believer's standing rests entirely on Christ's imputed righteousness, not on any righteousness of his own (infused or otherwise). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive threefold imputation as the structural backbone of the gospel: condemned in Adam, redeemed through our sin laid on Christ, justified through Christ's righteousness reckoned to us — the great exchange (2 Corinthians 5:21) at the heart of the gospel.

Latin imputare; Greek logizomai; threefold imputation (Adam's sin to posterity, believer's sin to Christ, Christ's righteousness to believer); the heart of the Reformation justification doctrine.
